filename: Worldwide Timing of Growth Faltering Revisiting.pdf
authors: Victora CG, de Onis M, Hallal PC, Blossner M, Shrimpton R
title: Worldwide Timing of Growth Faltering: Revisiting Implications for Interventions
countries: 54 countries pooled (5 WHO regions; AFRO incl. Ethiopia/Ghana/Kenya/Nigeria)
data_source: WHO Global Database on Child Growth and Malnutrition (52 DHS + 2 MICS)
main_outcomes: WAZ, HAZ, WHZ by month of age
wash_exposures: None (no WASH variable)

page_refs: Abstract; e473 (conclusions); Fig.4 (AFRO/SEARO faltering)

authors: Black RE, Victora CG, Walker SP, Bhutta ZA, Christian P, de Onis M, et al.
title: Maternal and child undernutrition and overweight in low-income and middle-income countries (Lancet Series 1)
countries: Global/LMIC (Africa, Asia, Americas regional breakdowns)
data_source: WHO/UNICEF/World Bank joint child malnutrition estimates (639 surveys, 142 countries); NIMS Bayesian model; meta-analyses of RCTs/cohorts
sample_size: Aggregated global/regional estimates; sub-analyses vary (e.g. 19-22 cohort studies for SGA)
wash_exposures: WASH listed only as one determinant in conceptual framework (Figure 1); no empirical WASH estimate
method: Narrative synthesis + population attributable fraction (PAF) calculations + Bayesian hierarchical modeling (NIMS) + meta-analyses
main_findings: Undernutrition causes ~3.1 million child deaths/yr (45% of all under-5 deaths, 2011); Africa only region where stunted child COUNT increased
key_numerical_results: 3.1 million deaths/yr; stunting affects >=165 million children <5 globally
thesis_interpretation: Motivates burden-of-disease scale; situates WASH as one 'nutrition-sensitive' determinant in standard conceptual framework, not itself WASH evidence
limitations_stated: Vitamin A/zinc mortality estimation uncertainty; explicit 'Panel 2: what this paper does not cover' excludes dedicated WASH empirical analysis
additional_limitation_for_our_design: Provides no regression design, FE, or exposure-construction precedent of any kind
page_refs: Key messages panel; Figure 1 (conceptual framework); Panel 1 (diarrhoea-stunting pooled analysis)

filename: Maternal and child undernutrition consequences for adult.pdf
authors: Victora CG, Adair L, Fall C, Hallal PC, Martorell R, Richter L, Sachdev HS
title: Maternal and child undernutrition: consequences for adult health and human capital (Lancet Series 2)
countries: Brazil, Guatemala, India, Philippines, South Africa (5 cohorts; none of thesis's 4 countries)
data_source: 5 prospective birth-cohort studies (Pelotas, INCAP Guatemala, New Delhi, Cebu, Soweto Birth-to-Twenty)
main_outcomes: Adult height, schooling, income, offspring birthweight, BMI, blood pressure, glucose, CVD
nutrition_measures: Maternal height, birthweight/IUGR, WAZ/HAZ/BAZ at 2 years
wash_exposures: None
method: Cohort-specific multiple linear regression (confounder-adjusted), pooled via random-effects meta-analysis (Q-test heterogeneity)
other_controls: Age at outcome, maternal/paternal schooling, childhood SES (asset PCA)
main_findings: HAZ at 2y is strongest predictor of adult human capital; 1 SD HAZ gain = ~0.50 more school years, 3.2cm more adult height (pooled)
key_numerical_results: Pooled: 0.50 school-years per 1 HAZ-SD (p<0.0001); 3.2cm adult height per 1 HAZ-SD
thesis_interpretation: Strongest evidence for why HAZ is the theoretically preferred primary outcome; entirely about downstream consequences, not WASH
limitations_stated: Observational, residual confounding cannot be ruled out; cohorts too young to assess life expectancy; glucose/BP associations inconsistent
additional_limitation_for_our_design: No WASH content, no DHS data, no country overlap with thesis; not a design precedent
page_refs: Key messages; Table 3 (pooled HAZ->schooling/height estimates); Discussion (observational caveat)

authors: Blom S, Ortiz-Bobea A, Hoddinott J
title: Heat exposure and child nutrition: Evidence from West Africa
publication: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management 115:102698
countries: Benin, Burkina Faso, Cote d'Ivoire, Ghana, Togo
data_source: DHS geo-referenced surveys linked to Global Meteorological Forcing Dataset (GMFD, 0.25 deg grid)
nutrition_measures: HAZ, WHZ continuous (primary); stunting, wasting, severe wasting binary (robustness)
wash_exposures: Household water source (well/piped/neither) and improved-latrine status used ONLY as controls, not the exposure of interest
geographic_level_exposure: Household-level controls; heat exposure at grid-cell (0.25deg) / region level
exposure_type: household-level (for the WASH controls specifically; heat exposure itself is grid/region-level, not WASH)
method: OLS with high-dimensional FE: cell x interview-month x interview-year FE (HAZ models); region x month / region x year FE (WHZ models, since clusters not repeated)
geographic_fe: Grid-cell x month x year (chronic outcomes); admin-region x month/year (acute outcomes) - explicit fallback due to non-repeated DHS clusters
other_controls: Child sex/age/birth size/eldest-status; mother age/education/height; household water/latrine/wealth; precipitation bins
weighting: Not stated as using DHS sampling weights in reported models
main_findings: Lifetime heat >35C decreases HAZ, increases stunting; recent (90-day) heat 30-35C decreases WHZ, increases wasting
key_numerical_results: 100hrs/month >35C: HAZ -0.17 to -0.30 SD; stunting +5.9pp (18% relative); +2C projected: stunting effect nearly doubles (4.0->7.4pp)
thesis_interpretation: Closest econometric analogue found: same DHS+geo-cluster framework, continuous HAZ/WHZ primary + binary stunting/wasting robustness tier exactly matches thesis structure; admin-region FE used specifically because DHS clusters aren't repeated across rounds - direct precedent for thesis's choice of region FE over spatial grid
limitations_stated: WHZ/acute models 'cannot be thought of as causal' (authors' own words) since clusters not repeated; GPS displacement 'has potential to bias estimates downward'; survivor-selection bias in youngest children possible
additional_limitation_for_our_design: Exposure of interest is temperature, not WASH; water/latrine are simple household controls, not cluster-level LOO exposure - does not validate the thesis's exposure construction, only its FE/tiering choices
page_refs: Abstract; Table 11 (water/latrine coefficients); Section 5.3 (single-country FE instability); Fig.8 (+2C projection)

authors: Gebru KF, Haileselassie WM, Temesgen AH, Seid AO, Mulugeta BA
title: Determinants of stunting among under-five children in Ethiopia: a multilevel mixed-effects analysis of 2016 Ethiopian demographic and health survey data
countries: Ethiopia
data_source: 2016 Ethiopian DHS (EDHS)
nutrition_measures: Stunting (binary only; no continuous HAZ regression)
wash_exposures: Community-level source of drinking water and type of toilet (aggregated individual data, simple improved/unimproved)
geographic_level_exposure: Community/cluster-level (aggregated), region (Ethiopia admin regions, fixed covariate)
exposure_type: community/cluster-level own-inclusive (built by aggregating individual household data; no LOO exclusion described)
method: Two-level multilevel mixed-effects logistic regression; 4 nested models; random community intercept
geographic_fe: Region entered as fixed categorical covariate (Addis Ababa=reference) alongside random community intercept
other_controls: Child age/sex/birth type/size; mother age/education/BMI/ANC/parity; father education; wealth; religion; community women's education/poverty
weighting: Sampling weights applied for descriptive/bivariate stage; NOT stated explicitly whether applied to the multilevel regression itself
main_findings: National stunting prevalence 38.39%; age 24-59mo AOR=10.00 vs 0-5mo; Amhara/Tigray/Benishangul higher odds than Addis Ababa
key_numerical_results: Stunting 38.39%; age 24-59mo AOR=10.00 (95%CI 7.71-12.98); water source AOR=1.05 (95%CI 0.90-1.22, NOT significant) in final model
thesis_interpretation: Ethiopia-specific DHS precedent for region-as-covariate and multilevel clustering handling; IMPORTANT null finding - simple binary improved-water indicator NOT significantly associated with stunting once other factors controlled, in Ethiopia specifically

filename: Acta Paediatrica - 2007 -  - WHO Child Growth Standards based on length height  weight and age.pdf
authors: WHO Multicentre Growth Reference Study Group (de Onis M, Martorell R, Garza C, Lartey A); statistical analysis by Borghi E
title: WHO Child Growth Standards based on length/height, weight and age
countries: 6 MGRS sites: Davis(USA), Muscat(Oman), Oslo(Norway), Pelotas(Brazil), Accra(Ghana), South Delhi(India)
data_source: WHO Multicentre Growth Reference Study (MGRS) - purpose-built prospective+cross-sectional study
study_population: Healthy breastfed infants/children screened for 'unconstrained growth'
main_outcomes: The growth-standard curves themselves: WAZ, HAZ, WHZ, BAZ percentile/z-score curves 0-60 months
wash_exposures: None
method: Statistical curve-fitting: Box-Cox power exponential (BCPE) distribution + cubic-spline smoothing via GAMLSS; 5 candidate distributions/2 smoothing techniques compared via AIC/worm plots
geographic_fe: None (curve-construction methodology, not a determinants regression)
other_controls: Eligibility screening (breastfeeding, non-smoking, no growth-constraining morbidity) as inclusion criteria
weighting: Not applicable (purpose-built study, not weighted national survey)
main_findings: Only ~3% of length variability attributable to inter-site (country) differences vs 70% within-site individual variability, justifying single pooled international standard

limitations_stated: Reference population deliberately NOT representative of general child populations (screened for unconstrained growth); cannot algorithmically convert old NCHS-based prevalence to new standard

authors: Cumming O, Arnold BF, Ban R, Clasen T, Esteves Mills J, Freeman MC, Gordon B, Guiteras R, Howard G, Hunter PR, Johnston RB, Pickering AJ, Prendergast AJ, Prüss-Üstün A, Rosenboom JW, Spears D, Sundberg S, Wolf J, Null C, Luby SP, Humphrey JH, Colford JM Jr.
title: The implications of three major new trials for the effect of water, sanitation and hygiene on childhood diarrhea and stunting: a consensus statement
countries: Bangladesh, Kenya, Zimbabwe (RCT sites)
data_source: 3 major RCTs: WASH-Benefits Bangladesh, WASH-Benefits Kenya, SHINE Zimbabwe
sample_size: Per-trial (not aggregated in this consensus statement)
wash_exposures: Basic WASH intervention packages (RCT-assigned, not observational coverage rates)
exposure_type: other/not applicable (RCT-assigned intervention, not an observational cluster measure)
method: Consensus statement synthesizing 3 cluster-randomized controlled trials
main_findings: ALL THREE major RCTs (WASH-Benefits Bangladesh/Kenya, SHINE Zimbabwe) found NO CAUSAL EFFECT of basic WASH interventions on child linear growth; mixed effects on diarrhea
key_numerical_results: Null causal effect on HAZ across all 3 RCTs (genuine causal identification via randomization)
thesis_interpretation: CRITICAL TENSION SOURCE: these are genuine causal (RCT) null findings on WASH->linear growth, directly in tension with a simple 'WASH improves child nutrition' motivating narrative; must be addressed explicitly, not glossed over, when interpreting the thesis's own cross-sectional associational estimates
limitations_stated: Basic WASH package intensity/duration may be insufficient; trials conducted in specific contexts (Bangladesh/Kenya/Zimbabwe) not generalizable without caveat
additional_limitation_for_our_design: These are causal RCT findings; the thesis's own design is explicitly associational/cross-sectional and CANNOT resolve or confirm/refute this causal null result - framing must acknowledge this asymmetry
page_refs: BMC Medicine 17:173 (whole article - consensus statement)

authors: Rakotomanana H, Komakech JJ, Walters CN, Stoecker BJ
title: The WHO and UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) Indicators for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene and Their Association with Linear Growth in Children 6 to 23 Months in East Africa
publication: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 17(17):6262
countries: 8 East African countries analyzed separately, including Kenya

sample_size: Kenya: n=3,978 final analytic sample (from 21,718 original -> 6,641 with WASH data -> 3,978 with complete anthropometry), Table 1 p.3
wash_exposures: Household-level WHO/UNICEF JMP water/sanitation ladder categories (improved/unimproved, further disaggregated basic/limited/surface-water or open-defecation/unimproved/limited/basic sanitation), coded from household-level DHS variables
geographic_level_exposure: Household-level (JMP ladder categories, individual household service level)
exposure_type: household-level (own-inclusive by construction; individual household measure - CONFIRMED via full-text deep read: no cluster/community-level aggregation used anywhere in this paper)
method: Country-specific/stratified multivariable linear regression: unadjusted -> adjusted for covariates -> adjusted for other WASH indicators
geographic_fe: Not applicable - country-specific separate regressions; no pooled model or admin-region FE used (p.4)

authors: Skoufias E, Vinha K
title: Community-level externalities in child health: Evidence from Sub-Saharan Africa
countries: 20 SSA countries including Ghana and Nigeria
data_source: Harmonized DHS via IPUMS-DHS
survey_years: Multiple DHS rounds per country, 2000-2018 (Table 1, p.4); data first accessed 2 April 2021
wash_exposures: Community-level 'fraction of households in cluster with improved water' / 'fraction of households in cluster with improved toilet' (Tables 3-8, pp.9-13)
exposure_type: community/cluster-level own-inclusive - CONFIRMED via exact quote (p.7): the paper explicitly discusses 'non-self means' (i.e. leave-one-out) as a known alternative practice in the literature but states 'In our analysis we calculate community level means based on the sample of households with children under 5 years of age' (own-inclusive), calling the choice between the two 'an empirical question' it does not resolve. NOT leave-one-out.
method: Correlated-random-effects/Mundlak hybrid decomposition of within- vs between-cluster effects (equations 4-8, pp.6-7)
geographic_fe: Not applicable - no country/admin-region FE; model uses CRE/Mundlak hybrid decomposition with survey year and month dummies instead (eqs.4-8, pp.6-7)
other_controls: Child age (7 categories), sex, first-born status, mother's height >160cm, roof quality, household size, number of children under 5, travel time to urban center, wealth quintile, year/month survey dummies (pp.5-6; Table 3 footnote)
weighting: Not reported - no mention of DHS/IPUMS sampling weights anywhere in the article; only intra-cluster-correlation-corrected SEs are used (Table 3 note, p.9)
main_findings: Community toilet coverage positively/significantly associated with child HAZ in URBAN areas (Table 7, p.13); in RURAL areas the linear between-cluster toilet effect on HAZ is NEGATIVE (Table 8, p.14, collinearity-flagged, see caveat p.12). A separate quadratic analysis of FEVER (not HAZ) in rural areas finds increasing returns to toilet coverage up to a ~59% threshold (Table 10).
key_numerical_results: The ~59% increasing-returns threshold applies to FEVER in rural areas (Table 10 col.2, p.14), NOT to HAZ. For HAZ specifically, the rural between-cluster toilet-coverage coefficient is NEGATIVE (Table 8, Hybrid-All col.5: -0.0723, t=-2.73, p.11); only the URBAN HAZ effect is positive/significant (Table 7, col.5: 0.1805, t=5.59, p.13).
thesis_interpretation: Closest empirical analogue to thesis in country overlap (Ghana+Nigeria), outcome (HAZ), and data source (DHS via IPUMS) - CONFIRMED Type B precedent (own-inclusive community exposure, explicitly NOT leave-one-out) for the thesis's cluster-level WASH exposure approach; must NOT be cited as validating the leave-one-out construction specifically
limitations_stated: Small-cluster-size attenuation bias discussed (pp.7-8); rural-area collinearity between within/between water and toilet coefficients flagged (p.12); 'the measure of improved water may not indicate safe water, especially if non-piped' (p.15)
additional_limitation_for_our_design: Own-inclusive (confirmed) vs. thesis's leave-one-out construction - distinct, explicitly acknowledged-as-different methodological choices; paper itself flags this as an open empirical question
verification_status: Verified (full-text deep read; exposure-construction question definitively resolved)
page_refs: p.6-7 (community-mean definition/equations 4-8); p.7 (non-self-means/leave-one-out acknowledgment quote); Tables 3-8 pp.9-13 (results)

authors: Addae HY, Sulemana M, Yakubu T, Atosona A, Tahiru R, Azupogo F
title: Low birth weight, household socio-economic status, water and sanitation are associated with stunting and wasting among children aged 6-23 months: Results from a national survey in Ghana
countries: Ghana
data_source: CONFIRMED via exact quote (Abstract, p.1): 'This is a secondary data analysis of the most recent (2017/2018) Ghana Multi-Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) datasets.' Data source is MICS, NOT DHS.
wash_exposures: Household-level binary: protected/unprotected water source; improved/unimproved/open-defecation toilet
method: Two-stage sampling (660 enumeration areas, p.3); complex-sample logistic regression (SPSS), bivariate then backward multivariate
geographic_fe: Not stated (adjusts for survey clustering/stratification, not admin-region FE)
weighting: Complex-sample design weighting applied (survey clustering/stratification adjusted)
main_findings: Bivariate: unimproved toilet -> wasting OR=2.01 [95%CI 1.05,3.85] p=0.035; open defecation -> stunting OR=2.07 [1.19,3.59] p=0.010; unprotected water -> wasting OR=1.97 [1.07,3.62] p=0.029. Multivariable wasting: unimproved toilet AOR=2.16 [1.03,4.55] p=0.042, unprotected water AOR=2.55 [1.22,5.34] p=0.013 (Nagelkerke R2=0.200). Multivariable stunting: improved toilet (vs open defecation) AOR=0.57 [0.37,0.88] p=0.011 (Nagelkerke R2=0.14); unimproved toilet NOT significant for stunting (AOR=0.99 [0.60,1.64] p=0.984)
key_numerical_results: Improved toilet AOR=0.57 for stunting (43% lower odds vs open defecation, p=0.011); unprotected water AOR=2.55 for wasting (p=0.013)
thesis_interpretation: Best available Ghana-specific WASH-anthropometric regression found - fills Ghana evidence gap, but CONFIRMED MICS data, not DHS - must be flagged explicitly as a different (though comparable, UNICEF-designed) survey program, not pooled with the thesis's own DHS-based estimates
limitations_stated: Exact quote (p.15): 'The main limitation of this study is its inability to infer causality of its findings due to the inherent limitation of cross-sectional studies'; birth weight based on maternal recall; 'A limitation attributable to the MICS not including an extensive number of nutrition-centred variables'
additional_limitation_for_our_design: MICS not DHS - different survey program (confirmed, not to be conflated); household-level exposure not cluster-level/LOO
page_refs: p.1 (abstract/data source quote); p.3 (sampling); Tables 3-5 pp.10-13 (results); p.15 (limitations)

filename: Forest cover associated with improved child health and.pdf
authors: Johnson KB, Jacob A, Brown ME
title: Forest cover associated with improved child health and nutrition: evidence from the Malawi Demographic and Health Survey and satellite data
countries: Malawi
data_source: 2010 Malawi DHS + MODIS VCF/NDVI satellite data (5km resolution)
main_outcomes: Severe stunting (HAZ<-3SD), dietary diversity, vitamin-A food consumption, diarrhea (2wk)
wash_exposures: None as primary exposure - household toilet/water access used ONLY as controls in the diarrhea model; primary exposure is forest cover (satellite-derived)
exposure_type: other/not applicable (environmental/geospatial exposure, not WASH; WASH vars are household-level controls only)
method: Unweighted multivariate binomial logistic regression (odds ratios)
other_controls: Child age, mother's education, urban/rural, wealth quintile, years resident, NDVI; diarrhea model adds toilet/water controls
weighting: Explicitly UNWEIGHTED (stated: 'we conducted multivariate analyses using unweighted binomial logistic regressions')
main_findings: Net forest-cover loss (2000-2010) -> 19% less likely diverse diet, 29% less likely vitamin-A food; higher forest cover -> lower diarrhea odds; NO significant stunting association with forest cover
key_numerical_results: Net loss: -19% diverse diet, -29% vit-A food; 50-59% forest cover: diarrhea OR=0.08 (P<.05); net gain: -34% diarrhea odds (P=.002); stunting: not significant (marginal P=.058 in unexpected direction)
thesis_interpretation: Direct precedent for DHS-cluster-GPS-linked geospatial exposure construction (though environmental, not WASH); explicit 'association not causation' framing precedent; the null stunting result (vs significant diarrhea/diet results) is a genuine unexplained anomaly the authors themselves flag
limitations_stated: Explicit: 'these preliminary findings demonstrate only associations, not causal relationships'; no water-quality testing despite hypothesizing water pathways; coarse 5km satellite resolution
additional_limitation_for_our_design: Exposure is forest cover, not WASH; unweighted, no PSU-clustering described - does not validate the thesis's weighting/clustering choices; only WASH content is as a control variable
page_refs: Results (dietary diversity/vit-A/diarrhea ORs); Discussion (associations not causal quote); stunting P=.058 anomaly

authors: Donohue RE, Church R, Assaf S, Mayala BK
title: Community Improved Sanitation Coverage and Childhood Stunting
publication: DHS Spatial Analysis Reports No. 23 (The DHS Program/ICF, official)
doi: No DOI (confirmed absent - The DHS Program does not assign DOIs to this document series)
countries: Nigeria and Zambia
data_source: CONFIRMED (p.2-3): 'This report uses data from the 2018 Nigeria DHS and the 2018 Zambia DHS.' Single DHS round only for each country.
study_population: Children (stunting outcome); households nested in DHS clusters
wash_exposures: Household-level improved sanitation (binary) AND community/cluster-level improved sanitation coverage (%, divided by 10 so ORs represent a 10-percentage-point increase)
geographic_level_exposure: Household + community/cluster (DHS cluster used as proxy for 'community'); region used only for a separate regional-breakdown analysis (Nigeria: six geopolitical zones)
exposure_type: community/cluster-level OWN-INCLUSIVE - DEFINITIVELY CONFIRMED, NOT leave-one-out. Exact quote (p.9): 'Community improved sanitation coverage was defined as the percentage of households within a cluster that have access to an improved sanitation facility...' Replication instructions (p.26): 'users can compute the community improved sanitation coverage by collapsing the data for each cluster and calculating the percentage of households...using an improved sanitation facility in each cluster' - 'collapsing the data for each cluster' is a standard own-inclusive cluster mean (includes the index household). The report never uses 'leave-one-out,' 'leave-out mean,' or 'excluding the respondent household' anywhere in its 53 pages.
method: Two-level mixed-effects (multilevel) logistic regression (Stata 'melogit', cluster as grouping structure), svyset multilevel/cluster-level weights constructed for complex surveys; run separately for Nigeria and Zambia (p.9)
geographic_fe: Not a fixed effect in the main model; region (six Nigeria geopolitical zones) used only for a separate stratified regional-breakdown analysis (Appendix Table 3)
other_controls: Not stated beyond household/community sanitation and regional stratification in the sections read (DHS SAR23 pp.1-5, physical pp.17-21)
weighting: DHS survey weights via svyset multilevel weights; cluster-level weights constructed with methods developed to estimate level weights for complex surveys (p.9)
main_findings: Nigeria: community sanitation coverage significantly reduces stunting odds overall (unadjusted OR=0.87 [0.85,0.89]; adjusted OR=0.97 [0.95,0.99]) - 'for every 10% increase in community-level improved sanitation coverage, the odds of stunting decreases by 3%' (p.18). Household-level sanitation significant unadjusted (OR=0.74) but NOT significant in the adjusted model (aOR=1.09 [0.94,1.26], Appendix Table 1 p.33). Regional breakdown: significant only in North West (aOR=0.95*, n=2,695, 275 clusters) and South West (aOR=0.94*, n=1,639, 235 clusters) of Nigeria's six geopolitical zones; not significant in the other four regions.
key_numerical_results: Nigeria adjusted OR=0.97 [95%CI 0.95,0.99] per 10pp community sanitation increase (Table 4, p.19); household aOR=1.09 [0.94,1.26] not significant (Appendix Table 1, p.33); North West aOR=0.95 [0.90,1.00], South West aOR=0.94 [0.88,1.00] (Appendix Table 3, p.35)
thesis_interpretation: Single most methodologically aligned candidate found in the entire gap search - a DHS-official, cluster-level community-sanitation-coverage variable regressed on stunting, in Nigeria specifically - BUT DEFINITIVELY CONFIRMED to be an own-inclusive cluster mean, NOT leave-one-out. Must be cited as a Type B precedent (community/cluster exposure) exactly like Skoufias & Vinha and Spears (2013), NOT as validating the thesis's leave-one-out construction. The mixed regional pattern (significant only in 2 of 6 Nigeria zones) is itself a genuine, noteworthy finding for the thesis's own discussion of heterogeneity.
limitations_stated: Exact quotes (pp.25-26): 'DHS data is only georeferenced to one location per cluster. Thus, the individual household coordinates are not available. Therefore, there is no information available on proximity to households that lack access to improved sanitation facilities.'; 'clusters may not always approximate communities'; 'we only evaluated a single DHS survey from two countries in this study, while many additional survey countries and survey years are available.'
additional_limitation_for_our_design: Own-inclusive, not leave-one-out - the exposure-construction gap this source was sought to fill remains open; multilevel random-effects approach (not PSU-clustered sandwich SEs) differs from thesis's clustering method; single DHS round only (2018), same cross-sectional limitation as thesis but no multi-round validation
verification_status: Verified (full-text deep read this stage, all 53 pages)
page_refs: p.9 (community sanitation coverage definition, model specification); p.26 (replication instructions confirming own-inclusive 'collapsing' method); pp.1-2 (cluster-as-community-proxy); pp.2-3 (2018 DHS rounds); Table 4 p.19 (Nigeria main results); Appendix Table 1 p.33 (household-level results); Appendix Table 3 p.35 (regional breakdown); pp.25-26 (limitations)

authors: Perez-Heydrich C, Warren JL, Burgert CR, Emch ME
title: Guidelines on the Use of DHS GPS Data
publication: DHS Spatial Analysis Reports No. 8 (The DHS Program/ICF, official)
doi: No DOI (confirmed absent - The DHS Program does not assign DOIs to this document series)
countries: Methodological; case study uses Uganda DHS 2011
data_source: DHS Program GPS/georeferenced cluster data in general
wash_exposures: None
method: Simulation studies quantifying displacement-induced bias for distance-based/raster/point-in-polygon analyses; Uganda 2011 DHS + poverty covariate case study
main_findings: CONFIRMED (p.44, bolded 'Proposed Guidelines'): 'we recommend that investigators implement a weighted average or most probable value approach when linking DHS cluster data to ancillary areal data. Misclassification rates are highly dependent on areal unit size.' Restated (p.48): 'probability-based approaches are recommended over simple point extractions' when 'areal units are relatively small.' Mechanism (p.40): buffer of radius = max displacement distance (2km urban/5-10km rural) per cluster; proportional polygon-area overlap used as weights (continuous data) or to assign 'most probable value' (categorical/admin-unit data).
key_numerical_results: Uganda case study (pp.42-43): first-level (larger) admin units - misclassification 4.5%+/-10.15%, no significant bias vs true (non-displaced) points; third-level (smaller) admin units - misclassification 32%+/-22% (5km rural buffers) to 55% (10km rural buffers), but 'very little bias was observed from naive analyses' due to strong spatial autocorrelation in the poverty covariate used - explicitly flagged as possibly not generalizable to weakly-autocorrelated covariates
thesis_interpretation: Official methodological justification for the thesis's approach of linking cluster coordinates to administrative regions - the thesis's admin-region level is coarser than SAR8's worst-case small-admin-unit simulation, closer to the low-misclassification first-level-admin-unit result, but SAR8's own explicit recommendation is a weighted-average/most-probable-value linkage rather than naive point-in-polygon regardless of unit size
limitations_stated: Exact quotes (pp.43,48-49): 'results obtained here are not necessarily generalizable because misclassification bias is also likely to be highly contingent on the magnitude of spatial autocorrelation in areal unit data'; 'Empirical results presented in this report correspond to worst-case scenario displacements, which are unconstrained by these [administrative] boundaries. Guidelines presented here are therefore likely to be conservative in nature.'
additional_limitation_for_our_design: Case study uses only Uganda/poverty, not any of the thesis's 4 countries or WASH variables specifically; guidelines are explicitly noted as conservative/worst-case
verification_status: Verified (full-text deep read this stage, core sections of all 88 pages)
page_refs: pp.39-46 (Ch.5, point-in-polygon analysis, complete); pp.47-49 (Ch.6 Summary, complete); p.44 (proposed guidelines); pp.42-43 (Uganda case study results)

title: Demographic and Health Survey Sampling and Household Listing Manual
publication: DHS Toolkit methodology series, document code DHSM4 (The DHS Program/ICF, official)
doi: No DOI (confirmed absent - The DHS Program does not assign DOIs to this document series)
countries: Cross-country/methodological
data_source: DHS Program sampling operations in general
wash_exposures: None
method: Two-stage stratified cluster sampling: PPS PSU/EA selection (cumulative-size systematic sampling, pp.64-67) then equal-probability systematic household selection within listed households (p.85)
main_findings: CONFIRMED (p.78, section 4.2): 'These software use the Taylor Linearization Method (Woodruff, 1971) of variance estimation for survey estimates that are means or proportions... The Jackknife Repeated Replication Method (Efron, 1982, 1993) is used for variance estimation of more complex statistics such as fertility and mortality rates.' Both formulas (p.78-79) are indexed/summed over strata h and clusters j within strata - the PSU is the resampling/replication unit, making PSU-level clustering the natural analogue for cluster-robust SEs. DEFT defined p.79: 'ratio between the standard error using the given sample design and the standard error that would result if a simple random sample had been used.' CRITICAL FINDING (pp.26-29, sections 1.13.5-1.13.7): explicit de-normalization procedure for pooled multi-survey/country analysis - 'the normalized weight is not valid for pooled data... because the normalization factor is country and sex specific' (p.26); exact formula given (p.28): HV005* = HV005 x (total residential households in country)/(households interviewed in survey), then re-normalize across the combined pooled sample (p.29). This section has NO counterpart in the Guide to DHS Statistics.
key_numerical_results: Not applicable (methodological formulas, not empirical results)
thesis_interpretation: DIRECT, CITABLE METHODOLOGICAL BASIS for the thesis's pooled equal-total-country weighting approach - the Manual's de-normalize-then-re-normalize procedure for pooled data is conceptually what an equal-total-country weight scheme accomplishes; also underlies the PSU-clustered SE choice via the Taylor linearization/JRR variance formulas
limitations_stated: Ch.4 'Survey Errors' (pp.73-79) states DHS surveys are subject to non-sampling errors (interviewer/respondent misunderstanding, data-entry errors, listing-to-interview timing gaps causing under/over-coverage, non-response) that are 'impossible to avoid and difficult to evaluate statistically' (p.73)
additional_limitation_for_our_design: Manual describes DHS's own official jackknife/Taylor-linearization variance software, not a generic cluster-robust sandwich estimator as commonly implemented in regression packages (e.g. Stata's vce(cluster)) - the thesis's PSU-clustered SE approach is analogous in spirit but not identical in implementation to what this Manual describes

page_refs: pp.64-67 (PPS mechanism); p.78 (Taylor/JRR variance methods); p.79 (DEFT definition); pp.26-29 sections 1.13.5-1.13.7 (pooled-data de-normalization procedure and exact formula)

authors: Gunther I, Fink G
title: Water, Sanitation and Children's Health: Evidence from 172 DHS Surveys
publication: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 5275
countries: 70 developing countries (172 DHS surveys); Ethiopia/Ghana/Kenya/Nigeria all included but only in older DHS rounds (1988-2008), no country-specific results reported
data_source: 172 standard-format DHS surveys, 70 countries
main_outcomes: Child diarrhea (2-week recall, binary); under-5 mortality (binary/hazard)
nutrition_measures: None (no anthropometric outcome anywhere in this paper)
wash_exposures: Primary: household-level categorical WASH technology indicators (latrine/flush/well-pump/piped vs open defecation reference). Secondary: an OWN-INCLUSIVE cluster-mean of WASH access used ONLY for an externality/spillover test
geographic_level_exposure: Household-level (primary); cluster-level own-inclusive mean (secondary, externality test only)
exposure_type: household-level (primary exposure); community/cluster-level own-inclusive (secondary externality-test variable - explicitly NOT leave-one-out, includes the surveyed household itself)
method: Logit (diarrhea) and Weibull survival model (mortality); country x year FE main models; region x year FE as OLS robustness only
geographic_fe: Survey-year x country FE (main); sub-national region x year FE (Appendix A.2 robustness only, due to computational limits in main Logit/survival models)
other_controls: Mother's education/age/marital status, household size, urban/rural, asset index, child age/sex/birth order/interval/breastfeeding, vaccination (diarrhea model)
weighting: Not stated in the specification sections (pp.16-18): the paper explicitly describes PSU-clustered SEs but does not mention DHS sampling weights
main_findings: Latrine/flush/well/piped access reduces diarrhea odds 7-17%, mortality hazard 5-20%; strong positive externalities for sanitation at cluster level (>2x household coefficient), NOT for water
key_numerical_results: Diarrhea: -7.3% (latrine), -12.9% (flush) [abstract]; cluster-level sanitation coefficient >2x household-level coefficient
thesis_interpretation: Genuine precedent for cluster-level WASH aggregation in DHS data, and for PSU-clustered SEs - BUT the cluster-mean is own-inclusive, used only for an externality coefficient-ratio test, NOT as a primary leave-one-out exposure, and outcomes are diarrhea/mortality, never anthropometric
limitations_stated: Cannot directly measure water quality (technology proxies quantity+quality); sanitation coefficients may partly reflect bundled hygiene-education; substantial coding simplification (400+ codes to 3 classes) risks misclassification bias toward zero; computational limits prevented region FE in main models
additional_limitation_for_our_design: Never uses an anthropometric outcome; cluster mean is own-inclusive, not leave-one-out - must not be cited as validating the thesis's exact LOO construction
page_refs: Abstract; p.18/36 (cluster-mean construction); p.26/36 Table 5 (externality coefficients)

authors: Spears D
title: How much international variation in child height can sanitation explain?
publication: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 6351
countries: Section 2: 65 countries (140 country-years). Section 3: India only. Section 4: India + DRC/Ethiopia/Kenya/Nigeria/Tanzania (Ghana NOT included)
data_source: Collapsed DHS summary statistics (Section 2); India NFHS-1/-2 microdata (Section 3); NFHS-3 + 8 African DHS surveys (Section 4)
study_population: Children (rural, under 3 for India district panel)
main_outcomes: Height-for-age z-score (HAZ), continuous - matches thesis's primary outcome type
nutrition_measures: HAZ continuous (sole outcome throughout, no binary robustness tier)
wash_exposures: Fraction of households in a village/PSU (or district, or country) reporting open defecation
geographic_level_exposure: Village/PSU (Sec.3/4, found significant); district (Sec.3, loses significance once village-level included); country (Sec.2)
exposure_type: community/cluster-level own-inclusive - no leave-one-out exclusion language found anywhere in sections read; reflection problem addressed differently, by entering household-level (own) and village-level terms JOINTLY rather than excluding own household from the village mean
method: OLS: country-year ecological regression (Sec.2); child-level regression with district+village terms and district FE (Sec.3); pooled India+Africa regression + Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition (Sec.4)
geographic_fe: Country FE + year FE + region-specific time trends (Sec.2); district FE + survey-round FE (Sec.3)
other_controls: ln(GDP), female literacy, nearby-water access, calorie deficit, polity scores, women's height, pop density (Sec.2); dirt floor, piped water, electrification, assets, mother's literacy/parity/religion, birth order, twinship, age-in-month x sex (Sec.3/4)
weighting: DHS sampling weights explicitly used throughout Section 4 (footnote 20); country-population weighting as alternative in Sec.2 plots; not fully verified for Sec.3

limitations_stated: Explicit: 'some fraction of these correlations also reflects omitted variable bias'; Simpson's Paradox risk in pooled cross-country regressions flagged explicitly; cannot fully rule out mothers'-own-stunting as alternative explanation
additional_limitation_for_our_design: Own-inclusive cluster mean, not leave-one-out; Ghana not covered in the Africa comparison sample (Section 4)
